issues.failure_explanation: The proof claims the substitution establishes V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}[G^{(\ell)}]^T[V^{(\ell)}]^T = I_{n_\ell}. Since V^{(\ell)} is n_\ell × r_\ell and G^{(\ell)} is r_\ell × r_\ell^0, the product is n_\ell × n_\ell and equals V^{(\ell)}(G^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)T})V^{(\ell)T}. With G^{(\ell)} having orthonormal columns, G^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)T} is a rank-r_\ell^0 projection, and V^{(\ell)}V^{(\ell)T} is a rank-r_\ell projection, so the product has rank at most r_\ell^0 < n_\ell and cannot equal I_{n_\ell}. The correct orthogonality to verify is (V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)})^T(V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)}) = G^{(\ell)T}V^{(\ell)T}V^{(\ell)}G^{(\ell)} = G^{(\ell)T}G^{(\ell)} = I_{r_\ell^0}.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $T_k(x) = \cos(k \arccos(x))$ denote the $k$-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind on $[-1,1]$,  which forms a sequence of orthogonal polynomials on $[-1,1]$ with respect to the weight $w(x) = 1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$.
The orthogonality property is based on the argument analogues to the  algebraic case but reformulated for polynomial arrays and note that the inner product should be properly weighted.

issues.failure_explanation: The claim is false on two counts. First, T_{0:m_\ell-1}(x_\ell)V^{(\ell)} produces r_\ell functions, not r_\ell^0. Second, even correcting the count, the functions are not orthogonal in general: the Chebyshev polynomials T_k are orthogonal but not orthonormal (‖T_0‖²=π/2 vs ‖T_k‖²=π for k≥1), so the Gram matrix of {Σ_i V_{i,j}T_i(x)}_j is VᵀDV with D=diag(π/2,π,…,π). This matrix is diagonal (i.e., the functions are mutually orthogonal) only if V preserves the two eigenspaces of D, which is not guaranteed by VᵀV=I. The proof's appeal to an 'analogue to the algebraic case' is invalid because the algebraic orthogonality (VG)ᵀ(VG)=I does not translate to functional orthogonality in a non-orthonormal basis.

failure_location.quote: If \cref{eqn:beta-Tucker} present the orthogonal Tucker tensor, then $\{T_{0:m_\ell-1}(x_\ell)V^{(\ell)}\}$ appear to be the set of $r_\ell^0$ orthogonal polynomials.
